newsitem.title: USA: Sprint to be sole sponsor of Rolling Stones tour.
newsitem.headline: Sprint to be sole sponsor of Rolling Stones tour.

text.p: In a bid to add some attitude to its image, telecommunications giant Sprint Corp. announced Monday it will be the sole sponsor of the North American part of the Rolling Stones' upcoming concert tour.

For Sprint, the nation's third-largest long-distance phone company, the deal offers the chance to raise its profile and provides a link to an enormously popular band. The Stones, in turn, will get an estimated $5 million to $6 million in the deal and plenty of wireless phones.

"It was obvious, the Rolling Stones and Sprint are a perfect fit," Sprint Chairman William Esrey told a packed outdoor news conference under the Brooklyn Bridge. "They were the original rock and roll rebels. Sprint is willing to break from convention and redefine telecommunications."

The core band -- Mick Jagger, Keith Richards, Ron Wood and Charlie Watts -- appeared at the event and announced that the "Bridges to Babylon" tour kicks off Sept. 13 in Chicago. The North America portion ends in February. An album with the same title was recorded last spring in Los Angeles and is set for release Sept. 30 on Virgin Records.

Sprint officials said the sponsorship will give them several ways to harness the Stones' marketing muscle. A tour logo even takes the pin from Sprint's "so quiet you can hear a pin drop" theme and sticks it square through the familiar protruding tongue of the Rolling Stones' logo.
The cost of all this to Sprint was not disclosed, but Tim Kelly, assistant vice president for advertising and sponsorship, said published reports of $5 million to $6 million were "in the ballpark."
"We wanted to do something provocative," Kelly told Reuters. "What better opportunity than this."
Kelly said a key element of the tie-in will be giving customers who sign up for Sprint service a chance to buy concert tickets ahead of the general public.

The company also will be allowed to use the Stones' image and music in television ads to be run regionally in the concert cities, Kelly said. Print ads touting the tour will run Tuesday in USA Today, he said.
Another benefit to Sprint will be availability of choice seats, which the company can use to entertain major corporate customers.
Sprint, based in Kansas City, Mo., will provide the Stones with a variety of telecommunications services such as wireless PCS, long distance and fax services.
Budweiser sponsored the last two Rolling Stones tours. Esrey said the Sprint sponsorship continues the company's strategy, which already includes the National Football League.
Kelly said the Stones' longevity -- this will be their 13th North American tour in 33 years and band members are well into their 50s -- has shown the band has broad popularity.
"The Stones are the pre-eminent rock 'n' roll band," he said. "They speak to a broad spectrum. It's rare to find a musical group that has that much appeal."

Sprint got a small, but immediate payoff, sharing the media spotlight with the Stones at Monday's event. More than 300 journalists from as far away as Poland and Brazil gathered under the bridge with the Manhattan skyline in the background and helicopters hovering overhead.

With Jagger behind the wheel, the four band members arrived in a bright red, 1955 Cadillac convertible after traveling across the bridge with police escort. "We're really pumped up for it," Jagger said.
